Train for the moment
the game asks more.
Cricket can give you time to wait. It does not always give you time to prepare.
The next ball can ask for a sharp acceleration, a hard throw, force through a shot or another demanding effort late in the day. Physical preparation has to make sense in that world.
This guide opens a window into the CAIRNOX approach: four sessions from the first week of a foundational training phase, with a purpose behind the work and a way to reflect on it.
Use the week to understand the structure, ask better questions and record the work. A single week is an introduction to the process. Development continues beyond these pages.

Mathew's experience spans USA Cricket, professional rugby, PSA Squash, British Cycling, professional soccer and NCAA programmes.
CAIRNOX brings that perspective to cricket: understand the player, understand the sport, then give the preparation a clear structure.
Start with what the work is intended to develop. Exercise variety is useful when it serves that purpose; it is not an objective of its own.
The gym shares the week with batting, bowling, fielding, practice, matches and travel. A programme has to sit inside that wider picture.
A clear session is one layer. Repeated work, recovery and adjustment connect the layers. That is where the longer development process begins.
This is Phase 1, Week 1 from the foundational strength plan. The day numbers show the source sequence; they are not four consecutive calendar days.
Put cricket in the diary first. Agree the session spacing with your coach before adding the training.
The four sessions follow the source order. Performance work leads, supporting resilience work follows, and conditioning appears where prescribed.
4 x 8 means four sets of eight repetitions. Distances and holds are written with their units. Exercise notes sit directly beneath the exercise.
Lettered codes preserve the source grouping. Do not assume a circuit or superset: confirm the intended order and recovery with Mat.
The source does not define ES / EL, the percentage load reference, most rest periods or a warm-up. These need Mat's instructions before independent use.
Use a sample as a sample
This week introduces the programme. It does not establish individual suitability or replace ongoing coaching. Do not turn an unclear instruction into a guess.

A bench press, a medicine-ball pass and a weighted chin-up occupy the performance block. The session then continues into supporting work and conditioning. Notice the structure: each block has a different job.

Record the work.
Notice the response.
A useful note is one you can return to. Record what you completed and anything that needs a conversation with your coach. A number on its own cannot explain the whole week.
Keep a fuller exercise-by-exercise record in your own training log.

What did this
week tell you?
Finishing the sessions gives you a record, not a verdict on your potential. The useful next step is understanding how the work fitted the player and the week.
Could you explain what each block was there to do?
What changed when cricket, travel or available time entered the picture?
Which question would you want a coach to help you answer before progressing?
